t: Japanese calm meets Scandinavian warmth.
d: Japandi blends Japanese minimalism and wabi-sabi with Scandinavian comfort and function. Low furniture, natural wood, muted earth tones and very little clutter create rooms that feel quiet and grounded.
o: The name joins 'Japanese' and 'Scandi'; the two traditions share a love of craft, nature and restraint, and the hybrid became widely popular from around 2018.
k: Light oak or dark walnut furniture
Hidden storage to keep surfaces clear
do: Edit ruthlessly: keep only what you love and use
Mix light and dark woods deliberately
Choose handmade objects over mass-produced decor
st: Clear every surface, then add back three objects
Swap a bright light fixture for a paper or rattan shade
Add one low wooden piece and a linen textile
w: Calm-seekers, small-space dwellers and anyone who loves natural materials.
b: Buy one well-made wooden piece and pair it with affordable linen and secondhand ceramics.

t: 1950s optimism: tapered legs, teak and clean lines.
d: Mid-Century Modern furniture is defined by organic and geometric shapes, tapered wooden legs, moulded plywood and a mix of warm woods with pops of mustard, teal or orange. It feels both retro and surprisingly current.
o: Design from roughly 1945–1969, shaped by American and Scandinavian designers and new manufacturing techniques.
k: Sofa or chairs with tapered legs
do: Mix vintage originals with modern reproductions
dont: Make every piece matching retro (it becomes a film set)
st: Add one piece with tapered legs
Choose a globe or sputnik light
Bring in one mustard or teal accent
w: Design lovers, collectors and retro fans.
b: Online secondhand marketplaces are full of real mid-century pieces.

t: Light, simple, cosy: designed for long dark winters.
d: Scandinavian interiors use white or pale walls, light wood floors, simple functional furniture and soft textiles to maximise light and comfort. Hygge (cosiness) is the emotional core.
o: Developed across Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Finland in the 20th century, with a strong democratic, functional design ethos.
st: Add a wool throw and sheepskin
w: Families and anyone who wants a bright, livable home.
b: Flat-pack furniture plus quality textiles gets you 80% of the way.

t: Rustic warmth with crisp, modern lines.
d: Modern Farmhouse pairs rustic elements (shiplap, reclaimed wood, barn doors) with clean, contemporary furniture and black metal accents in a mostly white and neutral scheme.
o: Popularised in the 2010s by home-renovation TV, updating traditional American farmhouse style.
dont: Add 'Live Laugh Love' style signs everywhere
st: Bring in a reclaimed wood piece
Swap busy decor for stoneware and greenery
w: Families who want a warm, practical home.
b: Paint and lighting swaps deliver most of the look.

t: Exposed brick, raw metal and loft-sized drama.
d: Industrial interiors celebrate raw structure: exposed brick, ductwork and concrete, paired with metal and reclaimed wood furniture and Edison-bulb lighting.
o: Grew from converting old factories and warehouses into lofts, notably in New York from the 1970s onward.
do: Show structure instead of hiding it
Warm it up with wood, leather and rugs
dont: Leave it cold with no soft textures
Fake it with cheap brick wallpaper
w: City dwellers and lovers of raw materials.
b: Salvage yards and restaurant-supply stores are goldmines.

t: Plants, pattern and layered global textiles.
d: Bohemian interiors layer rugs, textiles, plants and collected objects from different cultures and eras. The result is relaxed, colourful and personal.
o: Inspired by the free-spirited artists' homes of the 19th and 20th centuries and the 1960s–70s counterculture.
do: Layer textures and patterns in a shared palette
dont: Buy it all at once from one store
Ignore storage, or it becomes clutter
st: Layer a patterned rug over a jute one
w: Creative, well-travelled people who love colour.
b: Flea markets and secondhand rugs are the soul of boho.

t: Breezy whites, sandy neutrals and ocean blues.
d: Coastal interiors feel like a beach house: airy whites, sandy neutrals, soft blues, natural fibres and lots of light. Modern versions skip the anchors and shells for texture and calm.
o: Inspired by seaside homes in the US, Mediterranean and Australia; modern 'coastal' design moved away from nautical kitsch in the 2010s.
do: Let in as much light as possible
dont: Cover everything in anchors and seashells
w: Anyone wanting a calm, vacation feel at home.
b: Slipcovers transform tired sofas for little money.

t: Less, but better: space as the main material.
d: Minimalist interiors reduce furniture and decor to the essentials, using clean lines, a restrained palette and generous empty space. Every object is chosen for function or meaning.
o: Shaped by modernist architecture, Japanese Zen traditions and 1960s minimal art.
st: Remove 30% of objects in one room
w: People who feel calmer with less.
b: Minimalism is free to start: subtract first.

t: Jazz Age glamour: geometry, brass and velvet.
d: Art Deco is glamorous and geometric: symmetrical patterns, fan shapes, brass and gold metals, lacquer, velvet and bold contrasts like black and gold or emerald and cream.
o: Emerged in 1920s France (named after a 1925 Paris exhibition) and spread worldwide through architecture, cinemas and ocean liners.
st: Add a velvet chair in a jewel tone
w: Glamour lovers and entertainers.
b: Paint and hardware swaps (brass handles) give deco touches cheaply.

t: Heirlooms, symmetry and rich wood.
d: Traditional interiors draw on 18th- and 19th-century European design: dark woods, symmetry, detailed mouldings, rich fabrics and patterns like florals and damask.
o: Rooted in Georgian, Victorian and French classical styles.
do: Layer patterns in a shared palette
dont: Make it stuffy: add fresh elements
st: Add a pair of matching lamps
w: Lovers of history and formal comfort.
b: Antique furniture is often cheaper than new reproductions.

t: The sweet spot between traditional and contemporary.
d: Transitional design blends traditional comfort with modern simplicity: classic shapes stripped of ornament, neutral palettes and a mix of wood, metal and soft fabrics.
o: Became the dominant mainstream style in the late 20th and early 21st century as homeowners wanted timelessness without formality.
do: Mix one traditional and one modern element per room
st: Pair a classic sofa with modern lighting
w: Anyone who wants a home that never looks dated.
b: A neutral base lets you change accents cheaply.

t: What designers are doing now: sculptural, open and current.
d: Contemporary design means current design, so it evolves. Today it features sculptural furniture, curved shapes, open space, neutral bases and statement lighting or art.
o: Unlike 'modern', which refers to an early-to-mid-20th-century movement, contemporary is always of the moment.
st: Add a curved chair or sofa
Swap a lamp for a sculptural one
w: Trend-aware people who like a gallery feel.
b: Statement lighting delivers the most impact per dollar.

t: Warm minimalism: curves, wood and natural texture.
d: Modern Organic combines minimalist layouts with natural materials, soft curves and warm neutrals. Think limewash walls, bouclé, travertine and sculptural wood.
o: Rose in the late 2010s as a warmer, more tactile answer to cool minimalism.
st: Add a curved piece of furniture
Place a large branch in a vase
w: People who like minimalism but want warmth.
b: Limewash paint is an affordable way to get the texture.

t: Beauty in imperfection, age and simplicity.
d: Wabi-Sabi embraces the imperfect and impermanent: handmade ceramics, raw plaster, worn wood and natural fibres in earthy tones. It values patina, quiet and authenticity.
o: A Japanese aesthetic philosophy with roots in Zen Buddhism and the tea ceremony.
st: Replace a factory vase with a handmade one
w: Mindful people who love craft and calm.
b: Wabi-sabi favours old over new, so it's naturally budget-friendly.

t: More is more: colour, pattern and personality.
d: Maximalism layers bold colour, clashing patterns, art and collections to create rooms full of personality. Done well, a strong palette and repeated motifs hold the chaos together.
o: A reaction against minimalism, drawing on Victorian collecting and bold 1970s and 1980s interiors; surged in the late 2010s.
do: Repeat colours across patterns to unify
st: Paint one wall a saturated colour
Mix two patterns that share a colour
w: Collectors and colour lovers.
b: Paint and thrifted art give maximal impact cheaply.

t: Sun-washed plaster, terracotta and arches.
d: Mediterranean interiors evoke southern Europe: textured white or ochre walls, arches, terracotta tiles, wrought iron, wood beams and sea-blue accents.
o: Draws on Spanish, Italian, Greek and North African coastal architecture.
st: Add patterned tile or a tile-look rug
Bring in terracotta pots with herbs
w: Sun lovers and cooks who live in their kitchens.
b: Terracotta pots and limewash paint are inexpensive.

t: Old Hollywood glamour, high contrast and high shine.
d: Hollywood Regency is theatrical luxury: lacquered and mirrored furniture, velvet, bold colours, gold accents and high-contrast patterns like black-and-white stripes.
o: Associated with 1930s–50s Hollywood set designers and stars' homes.
do: Add shine with metals and mirrors
w: Entertainers and drama lovers.
b: Spray-painted gold frames and thrifted mirrors deliver glam cheaply.

t: Provençal charm: toile, curved wood and faded elegance.
d: French Country mixes rustic farmhouse comfort with refined French details: curved painted furniture, toile and gingham fabrics, linen, and soft colours like lavender, butter yellow and blue.
o: Inspired by farmhouses and manor homes of Provence and the French countryside.
st: Add a toile or gingham textile
Bring in a curved wooden chair
w: Romantics and home cooks.
b: Painted secondhand furniture is the heart of the style.

t: Nature-led rooms for better wellbeing.
d: Biophilic design connects people with nature indoors through plants, natural light, natural materials, water and organic patterns. It is linked with lower stress and better focus.
o: Builds on the 'biophilia' hypothesis (humans' innate attraction to nature) popularised in the 1980s, applied to architecture and workplaces from the 2000s.
do: Use natural textures you can touch
st: Add three plants of varying heights
w: Plant lovers and anyone who works from home.
b: Propagate cuttings to fill a room with plants for nearly nothing.

t: Granny chic, made fresh: chintz, wicker and scalloped edges.
d: Grandmillennial reworks grandmother-era decor (chintz, needlepoint, ruffled lampshades, wicker, blue-and-white porcelain) with a fresh, youthful eye and a lot of pattern.
o: Named in a 2019 article to describe millennials embracing traditional decor.
do: Mix patterns in a shared palette
dont: Let it look like a museum
w: Nostalgic decorators and pattern lovers.
b: Estate sales are packed with grandmillennial pieces.

t: Rough-hewn wood, stone and fireside comfort.
d: Rustic interiors celebrate raw, natural materials: rough wood beams, stone fireplaces, leather and wool, in warm earthy colours. It feels like a mountain cabin.
o: Inspired by rural cabins, lodges and farmhouses.
dont: Make it dark without enough lighting
st: Layer a wool or plaid throw
w: Outdoorsy people and cosy-cabin dreamers.
b: Reclaimed wood and secondhand leather fit perfectly.
